title: التغيّر مع مرور الوقت / Describing changes over time
bridge: In Arabic, changes are often expressed using structures like comparative patterns (أَفْعَل, afʿal) and particles such as أَكْثَر (akthar) followed by an adjective. A common mistake is translating 'cada vez más' literally as 'كل مرة أكثر' (kull marra akthar), when Arabic uses constructions like 'أصبح أكثر...' (asbaḥa akthar...) or 'ازداد' (izdāda...). Additionally, pay attention to the strict gender and number agreement of adjectives, which is more rigorous than in Spanish.
rule: To describe changes in Arabic at level B1, use these structures: 1) The verb أَصْبَحَ (asbaḥa, 'to become') + adjective in accusative or comparative, e.g. 'أَصْبَحَ الجَوُّ أَكْثَرَ حَرَارَةً' (asbaḥa al-jawwu akthara ḥarārah). 2) The verb اِزْدَادَ (izdāda, 'to increase') + noun or adjective, e.g. 'اِزْدَادَ التَّلَوُّثُ' (izdāda at-talawwuth). 3) Comparative patterns أَفْعَل (afʿal) for 'more', including feminine (فُعْلَى) and plural forms. 4) Phrases with 'قَبْلَ' (qabla, 'before') and 'بَعْدَ' (baʿda, 'after') to indicate temporal sequence. 5) The use of 'لَمْ يَعُدْ' (lam yaʿud, 'no longer') to indicate that something has ceased to be. Example: 'لَمْ يَعُدِ المَدِينَةُ هَادِئَةً' (lam yaʿud al-madīnah hādiʾah). When describing changes, Arabic frequently uses the passive voice or the verb 'صَارَ' (ṣāra) as a synonym for 'asbaḥa'. Ensure adjectives agree in gender, number, and case with the subject.

concept_examples.translation: The city has become more congested.

concept_examples.text: كَانَ الجَوُّ قَبْلًا بَارِدًا، أَمَّا الآنَ فَهُوَ حَارٌّ.
concept_examples.translation: Before, the weather was cold, but now it is hot.
concept_examples.phonetic: kāna al-jawwu qablan bāridan, ʾammā al-ʾāna fahuwa ḥārr.

concept_examples.translation: Students no longer write by hand.
The number of cars in the city has increased.

common_error.explanation: The error lies in using 'كُلَّ يَوْمٍ' (kull yawm) as 'cada vez' in a literal translation and placing the comparative without a change verb. In Arabic, 'cada vez' is expressed with 'كُلَّ يَوْمٍ' but requires a present tense verb or the verb 'asbaḥa' + comparative. The correct form uses the verb 'تَتَوَسَّعُ' (expands) or 'أَصْبَحَتْ أَكْبَرَ' (has become bigger). Avoid constructing the phrase without an explicit verb, as Arabic requires a verb to indicate a process of change.

levels.label: المُقَارَنَةُ بَيْنَ زَمَنَيْنِ
levels.translation: Comparison between two time periods (past and present)

examples.translation: The house used to be old and now it is new.
examples.note: Use 'كَانَ' (was) and 'الآنَ' (now) to contrast two states.

examples.original: سَابِقًا كَانَ القَمَرُ مَرْئِيًّا فِي النَّهَارِ، أَمَّا الآنَ فَنَادِرًا.
examples.phonetic: sābiqan kāna al-qamaru marʾiyyan fī an-nahāri, ʾammā al-ʾāna fa-nādiran.
examples.translation: Previously, the moon could be seen during the day, but now rarely.
examples.note: Learn to use 'سَابِقًا' (previously) and 'أَمَّا الآنَ' (but now).

levels.label: التَّغَيُّرُ بِاسْتِخْدَامِ أَصْبَحَ وَصَارَ
levels.translation: Change using أصبح (to become) and صار (to turn into)

examples.translation: The village has become a big city.
examples.note: The verb 'صَارَ' is used like 'asbaḥa' to indicate state changes.

examples.translation: Remote work has become common.
examples.note: Use 'أصبح' + adjective in accusative (asbaḥa + adjective) to express change.

examples.original: اِزْدَادَ عَدَدُ الزُّوَّارِ فِي المُتْحَفِ بِشَكْلٍ مُلْحَظٍ.
examples.phonetic: izdāda ʿadadu az-zuwwāri fī al-mutḥafi bi-shaklin mulḥaẓ.
examples.translation: The number of visitors to the museum has increased noticeably.
examples.note: Use 'اِزْدَادَ' (to increase) + noun + 'بِشَكْلٍ' to express degree.

examples.translation: The quality of local products has improved.
examples.note: The verb in form V (تفعّل) expresses qualitative change.

examples.original: قَلَّتِ المَسَافَاتُ بِسَبَبِ السُّرْعَةِ فِي النَّقْلِ.
examples.phonetic: qallati al-masāfātu bi-sababi as-surʿati fī an-naqli.
examples.translation: Distances have decreased due to the speed of transportation.
examples.note: The verb 'قَلَّ' (to decrease) is the opposite of 'اِزْدَادَ'.

title: التخمين والاستنتاج / Speculate and make deductions
bridge: In Spanish, to speculate we use modal verbs like 'puede ser', 'debe de', or expressions such as 'quizás' with the subjunctive. In Arabic, deduction is mainly expressed with particles like 'لعلّ' (perhaps), 'ربما' (maybe), and the verb 'قد' (may) followed by the imperfect. A key difference is that Arabic does not have a direct equivalent to 'debe de' for logical deductions; instead, it uses 'لابدّ أن' (must be) or 'من الممكن أن' (it is possible that), which changes the sentence structure. Additionally, while Spanish uses the subjunctive after expressions of doubt, Arabic typically uses the indicative imperfect (المضارع المرفوع) in most cases, avoiding confusion with the subjunctive.
rule:
To speculate and make deductions in Arabic (B1 level), the following structures are used:

1. **ربما (rubbamā)** + verb in the imperfect (المضارع) – equivalent to 'perhaps' or 'maybe'. Example: ربما يذهب غداً (maybe he will go tomorrow).
2. **لعلّ (laʿalla)** + noun or pronoun + predicate – equivalent to 'perhaps' or 'maybe'. Example: لعلّ الطقس جميل (perhaps the weather is nice). Note: لعلّ governs the accusative case for nouns if nominal, but with verbs, the imperfect is used.
3. **قد (qad)** + verb in the imperfect – indicates possibility ('may'). Example: قد يأتي متأخراً (he may arrive late). Also, قد + perfect indicates past possibility ('he may have come' – قد جاء).
4. **لابدّ أن (lā budda an)** + verb in the subjunctive (منصوب) – expresses strong logical deduction ('must be' or 'surely'). Example: لابدّ أن يكون في البيت (he must be at home).
5. **من الممكن أن (min al-mumkin an)** + subjunctive – 'it is possible that'. Example: من الممكن أن نسافر (it is possible that we will travel).

**Tense usage:** For deductions about the present, the imperfect is used; for the past, قد + perfect or لابدّ أن + perfect are used (لابدّ أنّه ذهب - he must have gone).

**Exceptions:** In colloquial Arabic, ربما is frequently used, but in MSA (Modern Standard Arabic), لعلّ is more formal. قد can be confused with the قد that means 'already' (e.g., قد فعلت = I have already done), but context clarifies the meaning.

**Common mistakes:** Spanish speakers tend to use the subjunctive after these particles, but in Arabic, the subjunctive is only used after أن (e.g., لابدّ أن), not after ربما or قد. They also often translate 'debe de' literally with يجب (obligation) instead of لابدّ.

concept_examples.translation: Quizás haga calor hoy
A lo mejor ella olvidó la cita
Puede que el director venga en un momento

concept_examples.text: لابدّ أنّه متعب بعد السفر الطويل
concept_examples.translation: Debe de estar cansado después del largo viaje
concept_examples.phonetic: lā budda annahu mutʿab baʿda s-safar aṭ-ṭawīl

common_error.wrong: ربما يكون الطقس حاراً اليوم (con subjuntivo en español: quizás sea)
common_error.correct: ربما يكون الطقس حاراً اليوم (correcto, pero con verbo en indicativo)
common_error.explanation: The most common mistake for Spanish speakers is transferring the use of the Spanish subjunctive to Arabic constructions that require the indicative. In Spanish, we say 'quizás sea', with the subjunctive, but in Arabic, 'ربما' is combined with the indicative imperfect (يكون). Do not use the Arabic subjunctive (منصوب) after ربما; it is only used after أن (e.g., لابدّ أن يكون). To avoid the error, remember: after ربما and قد, use the indicative (مرفوع); after لعلّ, also use the indicative (even if the noun takes the accusative case if nominal), and only after لابدّ أن use the subjunctive.

examples.translation: Quizás vayamos al mercado mañana
examples.note: Use of ربما with indicative imperfect for future possibility.

examples.original: قد يكون الجو بارداً في الشتاء
examples.phonetic: qad yakūnu l-jawwu bāridan fī š-šitāʾ
examples.translation: Puede que haga frío en invierno
examples.note: قد + يكون (imperfect) expresses general possibility.

examples.translation: Puede que haya olvidado mi llave en el coche
examples.note: قد + perfect (نسيت) indicates past possibility.

examples.translation: A lo mejor la lluvia para pronto
examples.note: لعلّ followed by a verb in the imperfect (without أن) for assumption.

examples.translation: A lo mejor tienes tiempo para ayudar
examples.note: When لعلّ is followed by a nominal phrase, the noun takes the accusative case (here, 'عندك' is a fixed expression).

examples.translation: A lo mejor han llegado al aeropuerto
examples.note: With the perfect tense, لعلّ indicates an assumption about a past event.

examples.phonetic: lā budda an takūna saʿīdan bi-n-natīja
examples.translation: Debes de estar contento con el resultado
examples.note: لابدّ أن + subjunctive (تكون) for logical deduction in the present.

examples.phonetic: lā budda annahum taʾaḫḫarū bisababi z-zḥām
examples.translation: Deben de haberse retrasado por el tráfico
examples.note: With the perfect tense, لابدّ أن expresses deduction about the past. Note the form 'أنّ' (with shadda) when followed by a pronoun.

examples.original: لابدّ أن هناك خطأ في الحساب
examples.phonetic: lā budda anna hunāka ḫaṭaʾ fī l-ḥisāb
examples.translation: Debe de haber un error en la cuenta
examples.note: Use with the particle 'هناك' (there is) – 'أنّ' is emphatic.

title: التعبير عن الندم والافتراضات / Express regrets and hypotheses
bridge: In Spanish, to express unreal hypotheses or regrets, we use conditional sentences with 'si' + imperfect subjunctive + conditional (si tuviera, haría) and structures like 'ojalá hubiera'. In Arabic, the most common structure is 'لو' (law) + perfective past + 'كانَ سـ' (kāna sa-) or 'لَـ' (la-) for the result. Unlike Spanish, Arabic does not distinguish between imperfect subjunctive and conditional; the simple past (perfective) is used for the condition, and the result is expressed with 'كان سيفعل' or the particle 'لَ' (la-). A typical error is to translate 'si tuviera' literally as 'إذا كان عندي' instead of using 'لو كان عندي'. Additionally, in Arabic the particle 'لو' (law) is used only for unreal or past situations, while 'إذا' (idhā) is reserved for real or future conditions; Spanish speakers often confuse these two particles.
rule: To express regret or unreal hypotheses in Arabic, use the structure: 'لو' (law) + verb in perfective past (الماضي) in the conditional clause, and in the main clause use 'كانَ سـ' (kāna sa-) + infinitive (for future or hypothetical actions) or 'لَـ' (la-) + perfective past (to emphasize the hypothetical result, often in literary sentences). Examples: 'لو كان عندي مال، لسافرت' (if I had money, I would have traveled) or 'لو كنت أعرف، لما فعلت ذلك' (if I had known, I wouldn’t have done that). To express regret about a past action, use 'ليت' (layta) + perfective past (meaning 'if only' or 'I wish'): 'ليتني درست أكثر' (I wish I had studied more). Another common structure is 'لو أن' (law anna) + nominal, meaning 'if (it were that)...' for counterfactual hypotheses. Exceptions: In spoken Arabic, the particle 'لو' is used similarly, but the construction with 'كان سـ' is simplified to 'كان راح' (kān raḥ) in dialects like Egyptian, or 'كان بيفعل' in Levantine; however, in MSA (Modern Standard Arabic) the construction is fixed. Do not use 'إذا' (idhā) for unreal conditions, only for real or future ones. To express regret, other expressions like 'يا ليت' (yā layt) for emphasis and 'ما كان يجب أن أفعل' (mā kāna yajib an af'al) for 'I shouldn’t have done' are also used.

concept_examples.text: لو كان عندي وقت، لسافرت إلى الأندلس
concept_examples.translation: If I had time, I would travel to Al-Ándalus.
concept_examples.phonetic: law kāna ʿindī waqt, la-sāfartu ilā al-ʾandalus

concept_examples.translation: I wish I had studied medicine.

concept_examples.text: لو لم أتأخر، لما فاتني القطار
concept_examples.translation: If I hadn’t been late, I wouldn’t have missed the train.
concept_examples.phonetic: law lam atāʾakhkhar, la-mā fātanī al-qiṭār

concept_examples.text: لو أنني عرفت الحقيقة، لتصرفت بشكل مختلف
concept_examples.translation: If I had known the truth, I would have acted differently.
concept_examples.phonetic: law annanī ʿaraftu al-ḥaqīqah, la-taṣarraftu bi-shakl mukhtalif

common_error.correct_alt: لو كان عندي وقت، كنت سأسافر
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish 'si' is used for all conditionals, but in Arabic you must distinguish between 'إذا' (idhā) for real conditions and 'لو' (law) for unreal or hypothetical ones. Using 'إذا' with the past is interpreted as a real condition, not a hypothetical one, and requires a result in the present or future, not in the conditional. Additionally, the result should include 'لَـ' (la-) or 'كان سـ' (kāna sa-) to match the hypothesis. To avoid this, remember: 'لو' + past + (la- or kāna sa-) for unreal hypotheses; 'إذا' + present/future for real conditions.

examples.translation: I wish I had listened to my mother’s advice.
examples.note: The particle 'ليت' (layta) is used for wishes and regret; it is constructed with 'ليت + pronominal suffix + past'. It means 'if only'.

examples.translation: I wish I hadn’t said that.
examples.note: 'يا' (yā) is added for emphasis. Negation is formed with 'لم' + imperfect (apocopate form) for the past.

examples.original: ما كان يجب أن أعامله بتلك الطريقة
examples.phonetic: mā kāna yajib an uʿāmilahu bi-tilka al-ṭarīqah
examples.translation: I shouldn’t have treated him that way.
examples.note: This structure expresses reproach/regret about a past action. 'ما كان يجب أن + verb' is equivalent to 'should not have done'.

examples.original: لو كنت مكانك، لفعلت الشيء نفسه
examples.phonetic: law kunta makānak, la-faʿaltu al-shayʾ nafsuh
examples.translation: If I were in your place, I would do the same thing.
examples.note: In Arabic, 'لو' is used with 'كان' to form the unreal condition. The result includes the particle 'لَ' + past (equivalent to the conditional in Spanish).

examples.original: لو كان الجو جميلاً، لخرجنا في نزهة
examples.phonetic: law kāna al-jaww jamīlan, la-kharajnā fī nuzhah
examples.translation: If the weather were nice, we would go for a walk.
examples.note: Here 'لو' indicates a counterfactual hypothesis in the present/future. The result with 'لَ' + past (denoting hypothetical action) is typical.

examples.original: لو كنت أعرف عنوانه، لبعثت له رسالة
examples.phonetic: law kunta aʿrif ʿunwānahu, la-baʿathtu lahu risālah
examples.translation: If I knew his address, I would send him a letter.
examples.note: The condition 'لو + كان + imperfect' is also used to express unreal hypotheses in the present. Note that 'أعرف' is imperfect, but with 'لو' it becomes hypothetical.

examples.original: لو لم أرَ تلك الرسالة، لما أخطأت في الجواب
examples.phonetic: law lam ara tilka al-risālah, la-mā akhṭaʾtu fī al-jawāb
examples.translation: If I hadn’t seen that message, I wouldn’t have made a mistake in the answer.
examples.note: In past hypotheses, 'لو لم' + past (negative form) and the result with 'لما' + past are used. 'لما' = 'la' + 'mā' to negate.

examples.original: لو كنا قد ذهبنا إلى الحفلة، لكنا قابلناها
examples.phonetic: law kunnā qad dhahabnā ilā al-ḥaflah, la-kunnā qābalnāhā
examples.translation: If we had gone to the party, we would have met her.
examples.note: The structure 'لو كان + قد + verb' is used for hypotheses about an unrealized past. The result with 'لكان + قد + verb' expresses the hypothetical consequence.

examples.translation: If you had told me about the matter, I would have helped you.
examples.note: 'لو أن + nominal' is a variant of 'لو' used before a noun or pronoun. It is common in MSA for emphasis.

title: مزايا وعيوب فكرة / Advantages and disadvantages of an idea
bridge: In Spanish we use connectors like 'por un lado/por otro lado' or 'aunque' to contrast pros and cons. In Arabic, the structure is similar, but we must pay attention to the conjunction 'لكن' (but) used to directly contrast, and the expression 'من ناحية... من ناحية أخرى' which is equivalent to 'por un lado... por otro lado'. Be careful with the word order in negative sentences with 'ليس' (not to be), which may differ from Spanish.
rule: To express advantages and disadvantages in Arabic B1, use structures such as: 1) 'من ناحية... ومن ناحية أخرى' (on one hand... on the other hand) to present two perspectives. 2) The conjunction 'لكن' (but) to contrast directly. 3) Verbs like 'يفضّل' (to prefer) and 'يعتبر' (to consider) to give opinions. 4) To negate, use 'ليس' (not to be) before a noun or adjective, e.g. 'ليس مفيداً' (it is not useful). In Arabic, the adjective comes after the noun and agrees in gender and number, unlike Spanish where it may vary. It is also common to use the expressions 'العيب هو' (the disadvantage is) and 'الميزة هي' (the advantage is) to introduce a specific point.

concept_examples.text: من ناحية، هذا الاقتراح مفيد، ومن ناحية أخرى، هو مكلف.
concept_examples.translation: Por un lado, esta propuesta es útil, y por otro lado, es cara.
concept_examples.phonetic: /min naːħija, haːða‿l-iqtiraːħ mufiːd, wa min naːħija ʔuxraː, huwa mukallif/

concept_examples.text: أعتقد أن العمل من المنزل له مزايا، لكنه يسبب العزلة.
concept_examples.translation: Creo que trabajar desde casa tiene ventajas, pero causa aislamiento.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʔaʕtaqid ʔanna‿l-ʕamal mina‿l-manzil lahu mazaːja, laːkinahu jusabbibu‿l-ʕuzla/

concept_examples.text: الميزة الأساسية هي توفير الوقت، والعيب هو قلة التفاعل.
concept_examples.translation: La ventaja principal es ahorrar tiempo, y la desventaja es la falta de interacción.

common_error.correct: هو ليس مفيداً، لكن الآخر مكلف
common_error.correct_alt: من ناحية، هو مفيد، ومن ناحية أخرى، هو مكلف
common_error.explanation: A common mistake is using 'و' (and) instead of 'لكن' (but) to express contrast. In Spanish, 'y' can connect two opposing ideas, but in Arabic, to contrast directly, it is necessary to use 'لكن' or structures like 'من ناحية... ومن ناحية أخرى'. Additionally, 'ليس' must be followed by an adjective in the accusative case (with tanwin) or a noun, and it should not be used directly with 'الآخر' without clear context.

examples.translation: The main advantage is the low cost.
examples.note: We use 'الميزة الرئيسية' (the main advantage) followed by 'هي' (is) to define.

examples.translation: This solution saves time.
examples.note: The verb 'يوفر' (to save) is common when talking about benefits.

examples.translation: It is good that the price is reasonable.
examples.note: The structure 'من الجيد أن' (it is good that) introduces an advantage.

examples.original: العيب الواضح هو أنه يستغرق وقتاً طويلاً.
examples.translation: The obvious disadvantage is that it takes a long time.
examples.note: We use 'العيب الواضح' (the obvious disadvantage) followed by 'هو' (is) and 'أنه' (that).

examples.original: ليس من السهل تطبيق هذه الفكرة.
examples.translation: It is not easy to implement this idea.
examples.note: To negate, we use 'ليس' at the beginning of the sentence.

examples.translation: There is a problem with this proposal.
examples.note: The expression 'هناك مشكلة' (there is a problem) is straightforward for pointing out a disadvantage.

examples.original: على الرغم من الفوائد، هناك بعض العيوب.
examples.translation: Despite the benefits, there are some drawbacks.
examples.note: The structure 'على الرغم من' (despite) is useful for contrasting.

examples.original: المزايا أكثر من العيوب في رأيي.
examples.translation: The advantages outweigh the disadvantages in my opinion.
examples.note: We compare using 'أكثر من' (more than).

examples.original: بينما يوفر المال، فإنه يسبب التلوث.
examples.translation: While it saves money, it causes pollution.
examples.note: The conjunction 'بينما' (while) introduces a contrast.

examples.original: رغم أن الفكرة جيدة، إلا أنها تحتاج إلى تحسين.
examples.phonetic: /raɣma ʔanna‿l-fikra dʒajjida, ʔillaː ʔannahaː taħtaːdʒu ʔilaː tahsiːn/
examples.translation: Although the idea is good, it needs improvements.
examples.note: The structure 'رغم أن... إلا أن' (although... however) is more formal.

translations.en: Advantages and disadvantages of an idea

title: سرد قصة أو حكاية / Narrating a story or anecdote
bridge: In Spanish, to narrate we use past tenses (preterite perfect, indefinite, imperfect) and connectors like 'entonces' (then), 'de repente' (suddenly). In Arabic, the verb system is different: there is no direct equivalent to compound tenses, and the particle 'قَد' is used for nuances. Additionally, Arabic marks the order of events with conjunctions like 'ثُمَّ' (then) and 'بَيْنَمَا' (while). Be careful: using 'كَانَ' + present verb can express an action in progress in the past, something that in Spanish is usually the imperfect tense. A common mistake is to translate 'estaba + gerund' literally using only the present tense, which sounds incorrect.
rule: To narrate in Arabic at B1 level: 1) The past is formed with the verb conjugated in the preterite (فعل ماضٍ). Example: ذَهَبَ (he went). 2) To express simultaneous actions in the past, use 'كَانَ + present verb' (was doing). Example: كَانَ يَأْكُلُ (he was eating). 3) Temporal connectors: 'ثُمَّ' (then), 'بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ' (after that), 'فَجْأَةً' (suddenly), 'بَيْنَمَا' (while). 4) The particle 'قَد' + past adds emphasis or indicates that the action occurred before another (pluperfect). Example: قَدْ زُرْتُ (I had visited). 5) Word order can be VSO (verb-subject-object) typical, but also SVO with emphasis on the subject. Avoid directly translating the Spanish compound perfect preterite ('he comido') as such; in Arabic, the simple past or 'قَد' is used. It is recommended to use 'كَانَ' for the past of the verb 'to be' in narratives.

concept_examples.translation: I went to the market yesterday.
It was raining while I was walking.
After that, we sat in the café.
Suddenly, we heard a strange sound.

common_error.explanation: A common error is using 'وَسْطَ' (in the middle of) instead of 'فِي' (in) for generic places; additionally, the explicit pronoun 'أَنَا' sounds emphatic but is not incorrect. However, the typical structure uses a conjugated verb without a pronoun. Also, 'أَكَلْتُ' indicates a completed action, but if you want to express 'was eating', you must use 'كَانَ + present verb'.

examples.translation: I visited my friend at his house.
examples.note: Use of simple past to narrate a specific event.

examples.translation: We drank tea in the garden.
examples.note: Past with plural (we).

examples.translation: The children played in the playground.
examples.note: Verb in past with subject after (VSO).

examples.translation: The weather was beautiful.
examples.note: كَانَ + noun + predicate to describe in the past.

examples.translation: The city was quiet.
examples.note: Gender agreement: كَانَتْ for feminine.

examples.translation: We used to live in a small house.
examples.note: كَانَ + present for past habits (imperfect).

examples.translation: First, I woke up. Then I had breakfast.
examples.note: أَوَّلًا (first) and ثُمَّ (then) to sequence events.

examples.translation: While I was reading, the phone rang.
examples.note: بَيْنَمَا introduces an action in progress (imperfect) and another in the past.

examples.translation: Suddenly, a strange person knocked on the door.
examples.note: فَجْأَةً (suddenly) adds surprise.

examples.translation: In the end, we returned home.
examples.note: فِي النِّهَايَةِ to conclude the story.

title: الدفاع عن رأي / Argue a point of view
bridge: In Arabic, to argue we use connectors like 'لأنّ' (li'ánna), 'بسبب' (bisabab) + genitive noun, or 'بما أن' (bimā an) + clause. Opinion structures include 'أعتقد أن' (aʿtaqidu an) 'I think that', 'أرى أن' (arā an) 'I see that', or 'من وجهة نظري' (min wijhat naẓarī) 'from my point of view'. Unlike Spanish, the verb 'to be' is often omitted in present tense, so you say 'يبدو' (yabdu) 'it seems' instead of 'هو يبدو' (huwa yabdu). Negation of nominal sentences requires 'ليس' (laysa) which agrees with the subject in gender and number, not the adverb 'لا' (lā) used for verbs. Spanish speakers often mistakenly use 'لا' for everything, leading to errors.
rule: To argue in Arabic, use causal connectors such as 'لأنّ' (li'ánna) + accusative noun/verb, 'بسبب' (bisabab) + genitive noun, or 'بما أن' (bimā an) + clause. For expressing opinions: 'أعتقد أن' (aʿtaqidu an) 'I think that', 'أرى أن' (arā an) 'I see that', 'من وجهة نظري' (min wijhat naẓarī) 'from my point of view'. Negation of present verbs uses 'لا' (lā) + verb, but negation of nominal sentences (without a verb) uses 'ليس' (laysa) which changes according to gender and number: ليس (laysa) for masculine singular, ليست (laysta) for feminine singular, ليسوا (laysū) for masculine plural, لسن (lasna) for feminine plural. Example: 'الرأي ليس صحيحاً' (al-raʾy laysa ṣaḥīḥan) 'the opinion is not correct'. In Arabic, the verb 'to be' is omitted in the present tense, so you say directly 'هو' (huwa) + adjective or noun. To connect contrasting ideas, use 'لكن' (lākin) 'but', 'بينما' (baynamā) 'while', 'من ناحية أخرى' (min nāḥiyat ujrā) 'on the other hand'. Arguments can be introduced with 'أولاً' (awwalan) 'first', 'ثانياً' (thāniyan) 'second', 'أخيراً' (akhīran) 'finally'. To conclude: 'لذلك' (lidhālika) 'therefore', 'بهذا الشكل' (bihādhā al-shakl) 'in this way'.

concept_examples.text: أعتقد أن التعليم هو أساس تقدم المجتمع.
concept_examples.translation: I think that education is the foundation of social progress.
concept_examples.phonetic: aʿtaqidu anna at-taʿlīma huwa asās taqaddumi al-mujtamaʿi

concept_examples.text: لذلك يجب أن نستثمر في المدارس.
concept_examples.translation: Therefore, we must invest in schools.
concept_examples.phonetic: lidhālika yajibu an nastaṯmira fī al-madārisi

concept_examples.text: من ناحية أخرى، قد يكون هذا مكلفاً.
concept_examples.translation: On the other hand, this might be expensive.
concept_examples.phonetic: min nāḥiyatin ukhrā, qad yakūnu hādhā mukallifan

concept_examples.text: لأنّ التعليم الجيد يحسّن فرص العمل.
concept_examples.translation: Because good education improves job opportunities.
concept_examples.phonetic: li-ánna at-taʿlīma al-jayyida yuḥassinu furaṣa al-ʿamal

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers tend to use 'لا' (lā) to negate anything, but in Arabic 'لا' is only used to negate present verbs or for negative commands. To negate a nominal sentence (without a verb), you must use 'ليس' (laysa), which functions as a negative copula and agrees with the subject in gender and number. 'غير' (ghayr) is also valid as an alternative to negate adjectives or nouns. The confusion comes from the Spanish structure 'no + verb ser', where 'no' is an invariable adverb. In Arabic, negation in nominal sentences requires a verbal form.

examples.translation: I think that teamwork is useful.
examples.note: The structure 'أرى أن' (arā an) is equivalent to 'I think that' in Spanish. Remember that the particle 'أن' (an) is followed by an accusative noun, here 'العمل' (al-ʿamal) carries the accusative marker even though it is often not pronounced colloquially.

examples.original: من وجهة نظري، السفر يوسع المعرفة.
examples.phonetic: min wijhat naẓarī, as-safar yuwasṣiʿu al-maʿrifa
examples.translation: From my point of view, traveling broadens knowledge.
examples.note: This expression is very common in Arabic. The phrase is followed by a normal verbal clause.

examples.translation: I believe that reading is a good habit.
examples.note: Note: 'أعتقد' (aʿtaqidu) means 'I think'. In Arabic, the verb 'to be' is omitted: you do not say 'هي تكون' but directly 'القراءة عادة جيدة'.

examples.translation: This opinion is not convincing.
examples.note: Use of 'ليس' (laysa) to negate a nominal sentence. Remember that the adjective takes the accusative case: 'مقنعاً' (muqniʿan).

examples.translation: Certainly, this is a good solution.
examples.note: The expression 'بالتأكيد' (bittākīd) is very useful for strong affirmation. It replaces the Spanish 'evidentemente'.

examples.original: لا أتفق معك، لأن هناك أسباب كثيرة.
examples.phonetic: lā attafiq maʿak, li-ánna hunāka asbābun kathīrah
examples.translation: I do not agree with you, because there are many reasons.
examples.note: Negation with 'لا' (lā) comes before the verb 'أتفق' (attafiq). Then 'لأنّ' (li'ánna) introduces the cause. Remember that 'هناك' (hunāka) means 'there is' and is invariable.

examples.original: رغم أن التكنولوجيا مفيدة، لكنها قد تسبب مشاكل.
examples.phonetic: raghma anna at-tiknūlūjiyā mufīdah, lākinahā qad tusabbib mushkilāt
examples.translation: Although technology is useful, it can cause problems.
examples.note: In Arabic, 'رغم أن' (raghma an) is used and then often 'لكن' (lākin) with a pronoun is added. This is a permitted redundancy but be careful with formal register.

examples.original: بينما يرى البعض أنها مضيعة للوقت.
examples.phonetic: baynamā yarā al-baʿḍ annahā muḍayyiʿatun lil-waqt
examples.translation: While some see it as a waste of time.
examples.note: The conjunction 'بينما' (baynamā) introduces a contrast. The verb 'يرى' (yarā) means 'he sees', but in this context it means 'opines'.

examples.translation: For this reason, I am in favor of the idea.
examples.note: Use of 'لهذا السبب' (lihādhā as-sabab) to introduce a conclusion. The expression 'مع' (maʿa) means 'with, in favor of'.

examples.original: بالنهاية، يجب أن نحترم جميع الآراء.
examples.phonetic: binnihāya, yajibu an naḥtarima jamīʿa al-ārāʾ
examples.translation: In the end, we must respect all opinions.
examples.note: The expression 'بالنهاية' (binnihāya) is equivalent to 'in conclusion, finally'. Structure 'يجب أن' (yajibu an) + subjunctive verb.

title: التحدث عن العمل والوظيفة / Talking about work and career
bridge: In Arabic, to talk about your profession or job, the verb 'to be' (like in Spanish 'soy profesor') is not typically used. Instead, nominal constructions or specific verbs like 'أعمل' (I work) or 'أشتغل' (I work/am employed) are used. Additionally, Arabic distinguishes between masculine and feminine in job titles (e.g., معلم / معلمة), similar to Spanish but with less regularity. Be careful with prepositions: in Arabic, 'أعمل في' (I work in) is used for places or fields, while 'أعمل كـ' (I work as) is used for professions.
rule:
To express your profession or job in Arabic, you can use the following structures:
1. **Nominal construction with 'أنا' + profession**: 'أنا معلم' (I am a teacher) for masculine, 'أنا معلمة' (I am a teacher) for feminine. The profession agrees in gender with the speaker.
2. **Verb 'أعمل' (I work) + preposition**:
   - 'أعمل في' + place or field (e.g., 'أعمل في مستشفى' - I work in a hospital).
   - 'أعمل لدى' + company or person (e.g., 'أعمل لدى شركة كبيرة' - I work for a big company).
   - 'أعمل كـ' + profession (e.g., 'أعمل كمهندس' - I work as an engineer).
3. **Verb 'أشتغل' (to work) is synonymous with 'أعمل' and is used in the same way.**
4. To talk about your career or trajectory, use 'مسيرتي المهنية' (my professional career).
5. When looking for a job, it is common to use 'أبحث عن عمل' (I am looking for work) or 'أبحث عن وظيفة' (I am looking for a job).
Note: Arabic does not use the indefinite article, so 'soy profesor' is translated as 'أنا معلم' without an article. Omitting the verb 'to be' is standard.

concept_examples.translation: I am an engineer.
I work in a big company.
I work as a doctor in a hospital.
I am looking for a new job.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, we say 'soy ingeniero' or 'trabajo como ingeniero'. When translating literally, many students say 'أنا أعمل مهندس' (I work engineer). In Arabic, you cannot use the verb 'to work' directly with the profession without the preposition 'كـ' (as). The correct forms are the nominal construction 'أنا مهندس' (I am an engineer) or 'أعمل كمهندس' (I work as an engineer).

examples.translation: I am a doctor.
examples.note: Use of nominal construction without an article for professions.

examples.translation: She is a teacher.
examples.note: Gender agreement: 'معلم' for masculine, 'معلمة' for feminine.

examples.translation: I am a lawyer.
examples.note: Example of an irregular feminine form: 'محامية'.

examples.translation: I work in a bank.
examples.note: Use of 'في' for a place.

examples.translation: I work in the field of education.
examples.note: Use of 'في مجال' to express the professional area.

examples.translation: I work for a small company.
examples.note: The preposition 'لدى' is used for employers.

examples.translation: I am looking for a suitable job.
examples.note: Verb 'أبحث عن' (to look for) + 'عمل' (work).

examples.translation: I want to develop my professional career.
examples.note: Structure 'أريد أن' + subjunctive; use of 'مسيرتي المهنية'.

examples.translation: I got a promotion at work.
examples.note: Simple past of 'حصل' + على; use of 'ترقية'.

title: وصف العمليات / Describing processes
bridge: In Spanish, to describe processes we use impersonal structures like 'se hace' (it is done) or the passive voice ('es hecho'), often combining phrases with temporal connectors such as 'primero' (first), 'luego' (then), and 'finalmente' (finally). In Arabic, the most common strategy is to use verbs in the first-person plural (نحن) or the passive voice (مفعول به) with the particle 'يتم' (it is carried out). A typical mistake is to translate 'se hace' literally as 'يفعل نفسه' (it does itself) instead of using 'يتم' or the passive form. Additionally, word order changes: in Arabic, the verb usually comes at the beginning of the sentence, and temporal connectors do not always appear at the start.
rule:
To describe processes in Arabic at B1 level, the following strategies are mainly used:
1. **Passive voice (الفعل المبني للمجهول)**: The passive form of the verb is conjugated in the third person singular or plural. Examples: يُغلى (it is boiled), تُقطع (it is cut).
2. **The verb 'يتم' + verbal noun (مصدر)**: This structure is equivalent to 'it is carried out' or 'it is performed' and is very common in Modern Standard Arabic. Example: يتم التسخين (it is heated).
3. **First-person plural (نحن)**: The first-person plural is often used to include the speaker: نحن نخلط (we mix), although in impersonal contexts the passive is preferred.
Important temporal connectors: أولاً (first), ثم (then), بعد ذلك (after that), أخيراً (finally). In Arabic, these connectors usually appear at the beginning or before the verb, but the verb remains at the start of the sentence in standard Arabic. Gender agreement is crucial: the passive participle or adjective must agree with the noun it refers to.

concept_examples.translation: Se hierve el agua primero.
Se precalienta el horno a 180 grados.

concept_examples.text: نخلط الدقيق مع البيض ثم نضيف الحليب.
concept_examples.translation: Mezclamos la harina con los huevos y luego añadimos la leche.
concept_examples.phonetic: naxliʈ ad-daqiːq maʕa l-bajd θumma nudiːf al-ħaliːb

concept_examples.translation: Después de eso, se deja enfriar la mezcla.

common_error.wrong: نحن نضيف السكر ثم يخلط نفسه.
common_error.explanation: The error comes from translating the Spanish construction 'se mezcla' (it is mixed) literally as 'mezclarse a sí mismo' (it mixes itself). In Arabic, the passive is formed with the verb conjugated in the passive voice without needing a reflexive pronoun. For 'se mezcla', you say 'يخلط' (yuxtalaʈ) or use the first-person plural 'نخلط' (naxliʈ) if it is more impersonal with 'we'. Avoid using 'نفسه' (itself) unless it is a truly reflexive action.

examples.translation: Se calienta el agua.
examples.note: Use of the passive voice of the verb 'calentar' (سخّن).

examples.translation: Se prepara la comida.
examples.note: Structure with 'يتم' + verbal noun (مصدر).

examples.translation: Cortamos las verduras en trozos pequeños.
examples.note: Use of first-person plural for process description.

examples.translation: Primero, lavamos las frutas bien.
examples.note: 'أولاً' is usually followed by a comma and often placed at the beginning.

examples.translation: Luego añadimos el azúcar y removemos.
examples.note: The connector 'ثم' (then) links two actions; the second verb is often preceded by 'و'.

examples.translation: Después de eso, se cuela la mezcla.
examples.note: Use of 'بعد ذلك' + passive to indicate the next step.

examples.translation: Finalmente, se pone la mezcla en la nevera.
examples.note: The adverb 'أخيراً' at the beginning and the passive 'يوضع'.

examples.original: يتم تسخين الزيت في مقلاة عميقة.
examples.phonetic: jutimm tasxiːn az-zajt fiː maqlaː ʕamiːqa
examples.translation: Se calienta el aceite en una sartén profunda.
examples.note: 'يتم تسخين' + complement of place.

examples.translation: Se añaden las especias gradualmente.
examples.note: Gender agreement: 'تتم' (feminine) because 'إضافة' is feminine.

examples.original: يُضاف الملح بعد أن يغلي الماء.
examples.phonetic: juḍaːf al-milħ baʕda an jaɣli al-maːʔ
examples.translation: Se añade la sal después de que hierva el agua.
examples.note: Use of passive 'يُضاف' + temporal subordinate with 'بعد أن'.

examples.original: نحرك المزيج ببطء حتى يصبح متجانساً.
examples.phonetic: nuħarrik al-maziːd͡ʒ bi-buʈʔ ħattaː jusˤbiħ mutad͡ʒaːnisan
examples.translation: Removemos la mezcla lentamente hasta que quede homogénea.
examples.note: Use of 'حتى' (until) + subjunctive in Arabic.

title: التعبير عن عدم اليقين والاحتمال / Expressing uncertainty and probability
bridge: In Spanish, you use the subjunctive (quizá, tal vez) or constructions like 'puede que' to express doubt. In Arabic, uncertainty is mainly marked with particles such as 'رُبَّمَا' (perhaps) and 'قَدْ' (may), which are followed by the verb in the present tense (المضارع). Unlike Spanish, there is no mood change: the verb remains in the indicative. Be careful with placement: 'قَدْ' sometimes implies weak or strong probability depending on context, and 'رُبَّمَا' is more neutral. 'لَعَلَّ' (maybe) is also used, which, unlike Spanish, requires a noun or pronoun in the accusative case after it.
rule:
To express uncertainty and probability in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA):
1. **Particle 'قَدْ'** (may): followed by a verb in the present tense (مضارع مرفوع). Indicates medium probability. Ex: قَدْ يَذْهَبُ (may go). It can also be used with the past to emphasize certainty, but at B1 level we focus on the present.
2. **Particle 'رُبَّمَا'** (perhaps, maybe): followed by a verb in the present tense. It is more neutral and common. Ex: رُبَّمَا يَأْتِي غَدًا (maybe he comes tomorrow).
3. **Particle 'لَعَلَّ'** (maybe, hopefully): followed by a noun or pronoun in the accusative case (منصوب), and then a verb or predicate. Ex: لَعَلَّ الطَّقْسَ جَمِيلٌ (maybe the weather is nice). It is closest to 'ojalá' in Spanish.
4. **Adverbial expressions**: 'مِنَ المُمْكِنِ' (it is possible), 'مِنَ المُحْتَمَلِ' (it is likely) + أن + present. Ex: مِنَ المُحْتَمَلِ أَنْ يَنْجَحَ (it is likely that he succeeds).
5. **The verb after these particles**: always in the present indicative, never in the subjunctive (as in Spanish). There is no mood distinction in Arabic for these cases. Exception: with 'لَعَلَّ', the verb is also in the present, but the subject is in the accusative.
6. **Negation**: to negate probability, use 'لَيْسَ مِنَ المُحْتَمَلِ' (it is unlikely) or 'مِنَ غَيْرِ المُحْتَمَلِ' (unlikely), or simply use 'لَا' with the present: لَا أَظُنُّ (I don’t think).

concept_examples.translation: He may be sick.
Maybe we will go to the cinema tomorrow.
Maybe the weather is nice today.
It is likely that the bus will be delayed.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers tend to put the verb in the subjunctive after 'quizás' or 'puede que' (vaya, venga), but in Arabic, the verb after 'قَدْ' and 'رُبَّمَا' remains in the present indicative, with no change in the final vowel. The only particle that requires the accusative case is 'لَعَلَّ', but it affects the subject, not the verb. So remember: do not look for a subjunctive mood in Arabic for these cases.

examples.translation: It may rain today.
examples.note: Used with the present tense for probable actions in the present moment.

examples.translation: She may be at home.
examples.note: With the verb 'كَانَ' (to be) to express a probable state.

examples.translation: I may travel next week.
examples.note: Note that the verb is in the present tense, not the subjunctive.

examples.translation: Perhaps he will eat the food.
examples.note: رُبَّمَا is more common in written and spoken language, with the present tense.

examples.translation: Maybe you understand the topic.
examples.note: لَعَلَّ + suffixed pronoun (كَ) in the accusative; then the verb in the present tense.

examples.translation: Maybe he will return soon.
examples.note: In Arabic, it is not a strict wish like 'ojalá', but a high possibility.

levels.label: مِنَ المُحْتَمَلِ وَمِنَ المُمْكِنِ
levels.translation: It is likely that / It is possible that

examples.translation: It is likely that the team will win.
examples.note: The construction 'أَنْ' introduces a subordinate clause, but the verb remains in the present indicative in Arabic (not in the subjunctive as in Spanish).

examples.translation: It is possible that she will not come.
examples.note: When the particle is 'أَنَّ' (with double n), the subject is in the accusative, and the verb remains in the indicative. Here with negation 'لَنْ'.

examples.translation: It is unlikely that we will succeed.
examples.note: To negate probability, we use 'لَيْسَ' before the phrase.

title: الطلبات الرسمية والكتابة الرسمية الأساسية / Formal requests and basic formal writing
bridge: In Spanish, we use '¿Podría...?' or 'Le agradecería si...' for formality, with the verb in the conditional. In Arabic, formality is expressed with structures like 'ممكن' (mumkin, 'is it possible?'), but in formal contexts 'أرجو' (arjū, 'I request/beg') or 'يُرجى' (yurjā, 'it is requested') are preferred, often followed by the subjunctive or a verbal noun. Note: the particle 'أنْ' (an) is essential to connect the verb after 'أرجو' (arjū). Also, the Arabic verb does not have a conditional like Spanish; instead, fixed courtesy formulas are used. A typical error is directly translating '¿podrías?' as 'يمكن' (yumkin) in overly informal registers.
rule: For formal requests in Arabic, verbs such as: أَرْجُو (arjū, 'I request/beg') + أنْ (an) + subjunctive verb (mansūb) are used, e.g., أَرْجُو أنْ تُرْسِلَ (arjū an tursila, 'I request that you send'). Also, يُرْجَى (yurjā, 'it is requested') is used for impersonal and formal written texts, followed by a verbal noun (masdar) or أنْ + verb. Another common formula: هَلْ يُمكِنُكَ (hal yumkinuka, 'is it possible for you...?') + أنْ + verb, but in formal registers 'أرجو' or 'يُرجى' are preferred. To ask for permission: هل يُمكنني (hal yumkinunī, 'is it possible for me?') + أنْ + verb. In formal writing, 'السَّيِّد' (as-sayyid) is used for Mr., 'السَّيِّدَة' (as-sayyida) for Mrs., and formulas like 'السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُم' (as-salāmu ʿalaykum) for formal greetings. The verb after أنْ always takes the subjunctive ending (-a). Exceptions: after 'يُرجى', a masdar without a verb can be used, e.g., يُرجى الإرسال (yurjā al-irsāl, 'sending is requested').

concept_examples.text: أرجو أن ترسل لي المستندات في أقرب وقت.
concept_examples.translation: Ruego que me envíe los documentos lo antes posible.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʔarjū ʔan tursil lī al-mustanadāt fī ʔaqrab waqt.

concept_examples.text: يُرجى التفضل بالحضور إلى الاجتماع غدًا.
concept_examples.translation: Se ruega tener la amabilidad de asistir a la reunión mañana.
concept_examples.phonetic: yurjā t-tafaḍḍul bi-l-ḥuḍūr ʔilā l-ijtimāʿ ghadan.

concept_examples.translation: ¿Podría hacer una pregunta?

concept_examples.text: نطلب منكم إفادتنا بخصوص هذا الموضوع.
concept_examples.translation: Les solicitamos que nos informen sobre este tema.
concept_examples.phonetic: naṭlub minkum ʔifādat-nā bi-khuṣūṣ hādhā l-mawḍūʿ.

common_error.explanation: The error is omitting the particle أنْ (an) after the verb أرجو (arjū). Spanish speakers tend to omit it because in Spanish we say 'ruego me envíe' without needing a conjunction. In Arabic, أرجو requires أنْ to introduce a verbal clause in the subjunctive. Alternative: use the masdar (إرسال) after أرجو without أنْ.

examples.original: أرجو أن تساعدني في هذا الأمر.
examples.phonetic: ʔarjū ʔan tusāʿid-nī fī hādhā l-ʔamr.
examples.translation: Ruego que me ayude en este asunto.
examples.note: Se usa أرجو + أنْ + verbo en subjuntivo (tusāʿida).

examples.original: هَلْ يُمكِنُكَ أَنْ تُجِيبَ عَلَى سُؤَالِي؟
examples.phonetic: hal yumkinuka ʔan tujība ʿalā suʔālī?
examples.translation: ¿Sería posible que respondas a mi pregunta?
examples.note: Uso formal de puedes con أنْ + subjuntivo (tujība).

examples.original: يُرجى التكرم بالرد في أقرب فرصة.
examples.phonetic: yurjā t-takarrum bi-r-radd fī ʔaqrab furṣa.
examples.translation: Se ruega tener la fineza de responder a la mayor brevedad.
examples.note: Se estructura con يُرجى + اسم مفعول/مصدر (التكرم).

examples.translation: Les rogamos que nos informen de su fecha conveniente.
examples.note: Se usa نرجو (plural de cortesía) para representar una organización.

examples.translation: Infórmennos de sus recomendaciones sobre esta propuesta.
examples.note: Imperativo formal (أفيدونا) en correspondencia profesional.

levels.label: صيغ رسمية في الإعلانات والتعليمات
levels.translation: Fórmulas formales en anuncios e instrucciones

examples.original: يُرجى عدم التدخين في هذه الأماكن.
examples.phonetic: yurjā ʿadam at-tadkhīn fī hādhihi l-amākin.
examples.translation: Se ruega no fumar en estos lugares.
examples.note: يُرجى + عدم (no) + masdar (التدخين) es común en carteles.

examples.translation: Por favor, sírvanse esperar en la cola.
examples.note: Combinación de لطفاً (por favor) con يُرجى + masdar.

examples.original: يرجى من السادة الموظفين تسجيل الحضور يومياً.
examples.phonetic: yurjā min as-sādati l-muwaẓẓafīn tasjīl al-ḥuḍūr yawmiyyan.
examples.translation: Se ruega a los señores empleados registrar su asistencia diariamente.
examples.note: Estructura يرجى من + sustantivo + masdar (تسجيل).

translations.en: Formal requests and basic formal writing
